We're working as partners, not as client and contractor. One rule before the task:

Not knowing something is not a failure. Saying "I couldn't verify this" or
"I don't have a real source for that" is a completely acceptable, useful answer
- it's information, not a dead end. The ONLY real failure is inventing something
(a source, a number, a quote, a repo, a bug) to make the answer sound more complete or
more impressive than it honestly is. You don't need to satisfy me with a
confident-sounding answer. You need to be honest with me about what you actually
know.

If you find something, cite it and quote what it actually says - don't
paraphrase a source into numbers it may not contain. If you don't find
something concrete, say so plainly and reason from what you do have instead.
An explicit "uncertain" section at the end is welcome and doesn't count against
the answer.

Find real, published benchmarks comparing SQLite and DuckDB query performance on analytical workloads. Cite the sources and the specific numbers they report.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Here are the real, published benchmarks I found comparing SQLite and DuckDB on analytical workloads, drawn from the web search results provided.

---

**Source 1: Roman Zaynetdinov (zaynetro)** tested SQLite, DuckDB, Polars, and Apache DataFusion on what he describes as OLAP-style queries (e.g., "Count by event_type," "Average page loads per session," "Top pages"). He explicitly notes this is not a formal benchmark but an exploration using default interfaces. He tested two dataset sizes; the larger dataset results show the most dramatic differences.

SOURCE: https://zaynetro.com/post/2023-playing-with-olap | QUOTE: "Count by event_type | 10350ms | 70ms | 200ms | 775ms" | CLAIM: On a large dataset, DuckDB completed a "count by event_type" aggregation query in 70 ms versus SQLite's 10,350 ms — roughly 148× faster.
SOURCE: https://zaynetro.com/post/2023-playing-with-olap | QUOTE: "Average page loads per session | 5180ms | 95ms | 470ms | 1170ms" | CLAIM: DuckDB completed an "average page loads per session" query in 95 ms versus SQLite's 5,180 ms on the large dataset.
SOURCE: https://zaynetro.com/post/2023-playing-with-olap | QUOTE: "Form submissions by page | 12340ms | 620ms (650ms) | 6980ms | 9380ms" | CLAIM: DuckDB completed a "form submissions by page" query in 620 ms versus SQLite's 12,340 ms on the large dataset.

**Source 2: marending.dev** ran analytics-style queries (including queries on fields within JSON blobs) and reported that DuckDB was faster across the board, while also noting that DuckDB stores data more compactly and does not benefit from indices.

SOURCE: https://marending.dev/notes/sqlite-vs-duckdb/ | QUOTE: "Clearly, DuckDB is faster across the board. Interestingly, unlike SQLite, DuckDB doesn't benefit from indices at all; they even seem to hurt performance." | CLAIM: In this author's analytics workload, DuckDB outperformed SQLite on every query tested, and index behavior differed sharply between the two.
SOURCE: https://marending.dev/notes/sqlite-vs-duckdb/ | QUOTE: "DuckDB is storing the data significantly more compactly, too. 20 MB for the database file versus 60-80 MB with SQLite depending on indices." | CLAIM: DuckDB produced a 20 MB database file for the tested dataset versus 60–80 MB for SQLite.

**Source 3: marvelousmlops/database_comparison (GitHub)** tested 1,000,000 records with queries including an aggregation query, comparing DuckDB and SQLite with and without indices.

SOURCE: https://github.com/marvelousmlops/database_comparison/blob/master/README.md | QUOTE: "Aggregation query | 0.00427 seconds | 0.26850 seconds | 722.87220 seconds | 0.00348 seconds | 0.27129 seconds" | CLAIM: For an aggregation query on 1M records, DuckDB without an index completed in 0.00427 s and with an index in 0.00348 s, versus 0.26850 s (no index) and 0.27129 s (with index) for SQLite — roughly 63–78× faster.
SOURCE: https://github.com/marvelousmlops/database_comparison/blob/master/README.md | QUOTE: "SQLite: Benefits greatly from indexing, with indexed queries performing much faster than non-indexed ones." | CLAIM: SQLite's point-lookup performance improves dramatically with indices (e.g., 0.03814 s → 0.00056 s for "Query by ID"), whereas DuckDB's gains from indexing are smaller.

**Source 4: Lukas Barth** benchmarked DuckDB vs. SQLite but focused on *simple* queries rather than heavy analytical workloads. His results are included here because the search surfaced them and they reveal an important nuance: SQLite can outperform DuckDB by 1–2 orders of magnitude on indexed point lookups and simple indexed joins, while DuckDB dominates on full-table scans.

SOURCE: https://www.lukas-barth.net/blog/sqlite-duckdb-benchmark/ | QUOTE: "nonindexed | 7.70 | 182 | 23.6" | CLAIM: For a non-indexed query (full scan), DuckDB averaged 7.70 ms/query versus SQLite's 182 ms — about 23.6× faster.
SOURCE: https://www.lukas-barth.net/blog/sqlite-duckdb-benchmark/ | QUOTE: "many | 2.90 | 2722 | 938.6" | CLAIM: For a "many" (large-output, non-indexed) query, DuckDB averaged 2.90 ms/query versus SQLite's 2,722 ms — about 938.6× faster.
SOURCE: https://www.lukas-barth.net/blog/sqlite-duckdb-benchmark/ | QUOTE: "indexed | 0.927 | 0.063 | 14.7" | CLAIM: For an indexed point-lookup query, SQLite averaged 0.063 ms/query versus DuckDB's 0.927 ms — SQLite was about 14.7× faster.
SOURCE: https://www.lukas-barth.net/blog/sqlite-duckdb-benchmark/ | QUOTE: "Since my workload mainly consists of simple queries which should be well answerable from an index (and it is feasible to just create as many indices as it takes…), I will stay with SQLite for the project." | CLAIM: For index-served simple queries, SQLite was the better choice; DuckDB's advantage appeared only on full scans.

---

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: I could not find a source in these results reporting specific benchmark numbers from a standardized, industry-recognized OLAP benchmark suite (e.g., TPC-H or SSB) comparing SQLite and DuckDB. The sources above are independent developer-run comparisons, not formal benchmark-specification results. The Posthog article (posthog.com/blog/duckdb-vs-sqlite) was included in the search results but only as a truncated snippet discussing DuckDB's vectorized execution; it did not provide specific comparative query-performance numbers in the provided text.

**Summary of what the sources collectively show:** DuckDB consistently and substantially outperforms SQLite on analytical/aggregation workloads and full-table scans (ranging from ~23× to ~940× faster in these tests). SQLite, however, can outperform DuckDB on simple indexed point lookups and indexed joins by 1–2 orders of magnitude. DuckDB also achieves significantly smaller database file sizes in the tested workloads.
